g.text: The source of truth is volatile. Every durable store is a projection of it.
Nothing on the critical path touches a database - an SSD read is 150 us against a 30 us budget. So this is storage DOWNSTREAM of the engine.
Four tiers of state - and the authoritative one is the tier that isn't durable
The structural claim: the EVENT STREAM is the source of truth and the relational store is a PROJECTION of it - the same CQRS
shape as the digital wallet, arrived at from a latency requirement rather than an audit one. And the order book, the thing
everyone calls 'the data', is deliberately NOT durable, because it is derivable.
The event stream is not a table - it is fixed 64-byte records addressed by arithmetic
struct SequencedEvent { // fixed 64 bytes = ONE cache line
uint64 sequence; // monotonic, from the sequencer
uint8 eventType; // NEW_ORDER | CANCEL | FILL | HALT
uint16 symbolId; // interned integer, never a string
uint64 gatewayTimestampNanos; // stamped ONCE, at the gateway
The record at sequence N lives at byte offset N x 64, so random access by sequence is POINTER
ARITHMETIC - no index, no parse, nothing to look up.
one cache line means reading a record is ONE memory fetch, not two. A variable-length
format (protobuf, JSON) would need an offset index AND a parse step - both on the hot path.
symbolId is a uint16, not a string
symbols are interned once at startup. Comparing and hashing a 2-byte integer is free;
comparing 'MSFT' is a length check plus a memcmp, and storing it blows the 64-byte budget.
float cannot represent decimal prices exactly, and a price comparison is what decides
whether two orders MATCH - so a representation error is a WRONG MATCH, not a rounding error.
no component downstream ever reads a clock: a clock read inside the loop would break both
the budget and functional determinism. It travels with the event, so replay uses it.
And what the sequence number does that a timestamp cannot: it IS the definition of priority.
Two orders arriving in the same nanosecond still have distinct sequence numbers, so price-time
priority is always unambiguous. Timestamps have resolution limits and clock skew; a monotonic
integer from a single writer has neither.
Off the critical path, ordinary relational modelling resumes
TWO rows per match, one per side -
the price is the RESTING order's
Columnar because every query is an
aggregate over one or two columns
and vectorizes the aggregation. A row
store reads every field of every row
In memory during the session because
and one day of 100 symbols fits in
RAM. After close it is cold - and cold
PRIMARY KEY (trading_date, order_id) - the schema's most consequential decision
a day's data is one partition, so dropping data past its retention
window is a DROP PARTITION - O(1) - not a DELETE of hundreds of
every real query prunes to one partition
1B orders/day x 7 years is ~2.5 TRILLION rows. Without a date-leading
key, 'this client's orders today' scans an index spanning all of
all of today's inserts land at the tail of one partition's index, so
there are no page splits across historical data.
This is the ONE place in this guide where time-based partitioning is right - the URL shortener, object storage and the message
queue all call it a write-hotspot mistake. The difference is the READ TAIL: there, a five-year-old short link is read as often
as a new one; here, yesterday's orders are essentially never read on the hot path. A write hotspot on the newest partition is
ONLY A PROBLEM IF THE OLD PARTITIONS WERE DOING USEFUL WORK. Being able to say why the usual advice inverts beats either
And the UNIQUE constraint is the most important
line in the schema. A broker supplies its own
client_order_id; one that times out and retries
sends the same one, the second insert violates the
constraint, and the existing order is returned.
Without it a retried submission becomes A SECOND
REAL ORDER IN THE BOOK - and a duplicate order that
fills is a position the client never wanted and is
legally obliged to settle. The critical path
enforces it in memory (the order manager holds the
day's id set); the constraint is the durable
backstop, exactly as the URL shortener keeps a
unique index it believes can never fire.
Deliberately absent: nothing on price or quantity - never searched by, only aggregated, and aggregation happens in the columnar
store. And no index at all on the event stream, because sequence x 64 byte arithmetic is the index.
Where the guarantees go - and the inversion that buys the latency
order books (in-memory) SERIAL, single-threaded one thread owns them, so no consistency model is needed at all - the
ABSENCE OF CONCURRENCY is the guarantee
event stream TOTALLY ORDERED, 1 writer the sequencer is the only writer, so the order is unambiguous by
construction. This IS the definition of what happened.
standby engine state BYTE-IDENTICAL to primary not 'eventually consistent' - identical, which is what makes
reporting store EVENTUAL, seconds behind lag is fine for reporting; a GAP is a compliance incident, so
completeness is monitored even though freshness is not
market data store EVENTUAL, sub-second rebuilt independently by the publisher, which doubles as a
positions EVENTUAL, recomputed intraday estimates for risk; authoritative at end-of-day settlement
The asymmetry worth naming: the strongest guarantee in the system -
total order, single writer - applies to an append-only stream in
VOLATILE shared memory, while every DURABLE store is an eventually-
That inverts the usual arrangement, where the durable store is
authoritative and caches lag behind it - and it is exactly what buys
the latency. The trade is that a total power loss with a
simultaneously-dead standby loses in-flight events, which is accepted,
and is the reason the standby is HOT rather than warm.
